# Final Experiment Design (design-only deliverable)

**Research question.** Does the adversarial game setup used in SPAG (imitation learning on GPT-4 followed by self-play on game episodes, instantiated as Adversarial Taboo) provide *superior* reasoning improvements compared to non-adversarial setups (20-Question, Guess-My-City)?

**Scope note.** This is a design document only. No experiment was executed, no results are reported, and no paper details are asserted as facts beyond what the task materials confirm. All source-derived facts are explicitly labeled; everything else is flagged as an assumption or a to-be-confirmed parameter.

---

## 1. Setup inventory: confirmed vs assumed

**Confirmed (from task materials):**
- Design-only task; `track.md`: "repositories and compute are not required." `/workspace` contains only `task.json`.
- The comparison structure is fixed by the question: adversarial arm = IL on GPT-4 + self-play on Adversarial Taboo episodes (SPAG-style); non-adversarial arms = 20-Question and Guess-My-City; outcome = reasoning improvements.
- Authoritative source for SPAG setup details is the NeurIPS 2024 paper #93638, available to the researcher via topics `setup_2`, `setup_32`, `setup_33`. Any paper-specific configuration below is marked **[ASSUMED — confirm via topic]**.

**Assumed (not confirmed by any available source):**
- Base model of LLaMA-2-class (7B/13B) **[ASSUMED]**; evaluation benchmarks BMATH and GSM-Hard **[ASSUMED — confirm via topic]**; two-role IL (guesser + word-giver) **[ASSUMED]**; iterative self-play with episode selection/filtering **[ASSUMED]**.
- The mechanics of 20-Question and Guess-My-City and whether their published training pipelines used IL+self-play — not available; the design *imposes* a symmetric pipeline on all arms (see §3, Assumption A2).

---

## 2. Arms (arm structure retained from approved skeleton)

| Arm | Game | IL (GPT-4) | Self-play | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Adversarial Taboo (SPAG) | yes | yes | core |
| A2 | 20-Question | yes | yes | core |
| A3 | Guess-My-City | yes | yes | core |
| C0 | no game training (control) | no | no | core |
| A1b | Adversarial Taboo, self-play only (no IL) | no | yes | **optional, priority 1** |
| A1c | Adversarial Taboo, IL only (no self-play) | yes | no | **optional, priority 2** |
| C0b | neutral SFT (matched token count, non-game data) | — | — | **optional, priority 3** |

Rationale for decomposition arms: A1b isolates the contribution of adversarial self-play per se; A1c isolates the contribution of GPT-4 imitation. If budget is tight, A1b first (it most directly tests "adversarial self-play is the active ingredient"), then A1c, then C0b. If even one optional arm is dropped, the conclusion must be phrased as "SPAG pipeline vs non-adversarial pipelines" rather than "adversarial self-play is the mechanism."

---

## 3. Justification of key design choices

**(a) Identical episode/token/iteration budgets across arms.** Training quantity is a confounder: more game episodes or more fine-tuning tokens mechanically improves benchmark performance regardless of game type. If arms differed in budget, any observed difference would be attributable to scale of training, not to adversarial vs non-adversarial structure. Therefore: identical number of self-play iterations, identical total fine-tuning tokens (IL + self-play combined), identical data-selection procedures, identical learning-rate schedule, identical decoding parameters at evaluation. Token budgets are matched at the *fine-tuning token* level (not episode count), because average episode length differs across games and episode-count matching would silently create token-count differences.

**(b) GPT-4 imitation held symmetric across arms.** The question fixes IL-on-GPT-4 only for the SPAG arm. Applying IL to all game arms is **Assumption A1** — a deliberate design choice, not a source claim. Justification: if IL were asymmetric, arm differences would conflate (i) game type with (ii) teacher-trajectory exposure. Symmetric IL makes the contrast a clean test of the game structure (adversarial opponent vs cooperative/informational game) under an otherwise identical curriculum. Consequence to acknowledge: a negative result would mean "adversarial games are not superior *under symmetric IL conditions*," not that SPAG's exact recipe (which may rely on the adversarial game specifically for IL) fails. If the researcher's topics reveal that IL is structurally tied to the adversarial game (e.g., GPT-4 trajectories exist only for Taboo), the fallback is to generate GPT-4 trajectories for 20-Question and Guess-My-City under the same prompting template — this becomes a stated assumption to validate in the pilot.

**(c) Superiority test paired with an equivalence check (TOST).** The question is phrased "does A provide superior improvements?" A one-sided superiority test alone cannot distinguish "no difference" from "underpowered study." Pairing a superiority test (one-sided, corrected for multiplicity) with two one-sided tests (TOST) against a pre-registered equivalence margin δ yields a complete 2×2 decision structure: (i) superiority demonstrated; (ii) equivalence demonstrated (adversarial offers no meaningful advantage); (iii) inconclusive (increase power or report honestly). δ should be set a priori, e.g., δ = 1 percentage point accuracy on the primary benchmark composite, or justified by the smallest effect that would matter for a practitioner.

---

## 4. Addressing the cross-game difficulty/length confounder head-on

The games differ in episode complexity, turn structure, and utterance length; without control, a "better" arm may simply train on more informative or longer text.

**Primary control — difficulty/quality matching of training episodes:**
- Define a per-episode quality/difficulty score common to all games: e.g., number of informative turns, episode outcome quality (win/loss plus margin), and a learned or heuristic measure of linguistic complexity (token length distribution, vocabulary level). Match the *distributions* of these statistics across arms by stratified sampling of training episodes (quantile matching on length and outcome rates), so each arm consumes episodes with comparable statistical profiles.
- Additionally match outcome-rate targets: cap each arm's training set so that (for example) the fraction of successful episodes is equalized, preventing one arm from learning mostly from wins and another mostly from losses.

**Secondary control — matched token budgets** (§3a) at both SFT and self-play stages.

**Fallback if distribution matching is not feasible** (e.g., a game's episode distribution cannot reach the target profile): (i) reweight episodes (importance weights) instead of hard matching, and report both reweighted and unmatched results; (ii) if reweighting also fails, include game difficulty as a covariate in the analysis model (ANCOVA-style: benchmark gain ~ arm + episode-difficulty covariates) and pre-register that the primary conclusion uses the covariate-adjusted comparison; (iii) in all fallback cases, report the achieved distribution mismatch statistics transparently as a limitation. The pilot phase (§7) measures whether matching is feasible before full scale-up.

---

## 5. Metrics

**Primary metric:** Δaccuracy on a pre-registered reasoning benchmark composite vs arm C0 (benchmark set is a to-be-confirmed parameter; candidate set BMATH + GSM-Hard is **[ASSUMED]**). The composite is the pre-weighted mean across benchmarks; per-benchmark deltas are secondary to avoid cherry-picking.

**Secondary metrics:**
- pass@k and self-consistency accuracy (reasoning robustness, not just greedy accuracy);
- CoT quality: step-verifiability rate (programmatic verification where possible, e.g., final-answer consistency; human/LLM-judge audit on a fixed sample), CoT length and repetition statistics;
- in-game performance: win rate per game for each arm playing *its own* game (verifies each pipeline actually improved at its game — a manipulation check), plus cross-game win rate where rules allow (transfer probe);
- mediator measures: fraction of utterances that are information-seeking questions vs disinformation-resistant behavior, to interpret *why* an arm gains.

**Manipulation checks (pre-registered):** (i) training loss/episode-selection statistics comparable across arms; (ii) matched-budget verification (token counts within tolerance); (iii) every trained arm must improve at its own game over C0 — if not, the pipeline failed and the arm's benchmark result is interpreted cautiously.

---

## 6. Analysis plan

1. **Seeds and power:** ≥3 independent seeds per arm (training seeds; evaluation is deterministic given decoding params). Pre-compute power from pilot variance estimates; target ≥80% power for the equivalence margin δ and for the primary pairwise contrast.
2. **Primary analysis:** per-benchmark-item paired comparison of each arm vs C0 (items are the pairing unit; cluster-robust or bootstrap CIs over items × seeds). Family of primary contrasts: {A1, A2, A3} vs C0 — Holm correction across the three.
3. **Key contrast (the question itself):** A1 vs max(A2, A3) — one-sided superiority test, plus TOST equivalence at margin δ. Decision rule: superiority claimed only if both Holm-corrected significance and practical magnitude (≥δ) hold; otherwise report "no demonstrated superiority" with the equivalence verdict.
4. **Decomposition (if optional arms run):** planned contrasts A1 vs A1b (self-play effect), A1 vs A1c (IL effect), both vs C0, Holm-corrected.
5. **Covariate-adjusted analysis** if the fallback in §4 triggers: arm effect adjusted for episode-difficulty covariates.
6. **Sensitivity analyses:** leave-one-benchmark-out; effect of episode-matching method (matched vs reweighted vs unmatched); seed-level leave-one-out to detect driver seeds.
7. **Reporting:** all contrasts with effect sizes (accuracy deltas, CIs), no outcome-dependent metric selection; null/negative results reported with CIs, not suppressed.

---

## 7. Feasibility and parametrized budget plan (design-only; no execution claimed)

Scope is design-only per `track.md`; the following is a planning framework, not performed work. All quantities are parameters (P1–P5) to be fixed once source topics confirm the SPAG configuration:

- **P1 — base model & scale** [ASSUMED: LLaMA-2-class 7B]: sets GPU cost per fine-tune; 4 core arms × 3 seeds = 12 fine-tune runs minimum (plus optional arms).
- **P2 — GPT-4 teacher budget**: cost driver for IL trajectories; scales as (games × episodes per game × tokens per episode). Symmetric IL (Assumption A1) triples teacher cost relative to SPAG-only IL; if budget-constrained, the first concession is to reduce teacher-episode count uniformly across arms, never asymmetrically.
- **P3 — self-play iterations** [ASSUMED: iterative, with filtering]: each iteration requires generation + selection + fine-tune; total cost = arms × seeds × iterations. Pilot (reduced scale: 1 seed, 2 arms, 1/10 episodes) validates the pipeline and estimates variance for the power calculation before full scale-up.
- **P4 — evaluation budget**: benchmark inference is comparatively cheap and cacheable; fixed decoding parameters.
- **P5 — pilot gate**: difficulty-matching feasibility (§4) and per-arm in-game improvement (§5 manipulation check) must both pass in the pilot before committing full budget.

**Practical constraints acknowledged:** environment has no GPU and no preinstalled dependencies; if execution were ever commissioned, infrastructure (fine-tuning stack, game servers for the three games, benchmark harness) must be built first — this is explicitly out of scope here.

---

## 8. Assumptions (separate from fixed task requirements)

- **A1 (stated per researcher comment #2):** GPT-4 imitation learning is applied symmetrically across all game arms; the question fixes it only for the SPAG arm. This is a design choice for causal cleanliness, not a source claim.
- **A2:** 20-Question and Guess-My-City can be trained with an IL+self-play pipeline analogous to SPAG's; their rules are implementable in the same interface.
- **A3:** Base model is LLaMA-2-class; benchmarks include BMATH/GSM-Hard **[ASSUMED — confirm via topic]**.
- **A4:** Reasoning improvement is operationalized as benchmark accuracy gain (not in-game skill per se).

## 9. Limitations and open uncertainties

1. **Unconfirmed SPAG specifics** (model, iteration/episode counts, data filtering, benchmark set): resolved only via topics setup_2/32/33; until then, all paper-derived parameters above remain assumptions.
2. **Non-adversarial game pipelines:** the imposed symmetric pipeline may not match how these games were trained in their original works; results speak to the symmetric-pipeline comparison, not to a reproduction of any original non-adversarial method.
3. **Residual difficulty confounding:** even with matching/reweighting, "episodes of equal statistics" need not be "episodes of equal learning value"; the covariate adjustment and sensitivity analyses mitigate but do not eliminate this.
4. **Teacher-quality confounder:** if GPT-4 trajectories are naturally higher-quality for one game (e.g., Taboo is better within GPT-4's strengths), arm differences partly reflect teacher fit, not adversariality; a game-teacher cross table (best-effort, optional) would be needed to probe this.
5. **Generalization:** conclusions hold for the chosen base model and benchmark composite; transfer to other scales or benchmark families is untested within this design.
6. **Equivalence margin δ** is a judgment call; the design pre-registers it but its defensibility depends on domain input.
7. **Statistical power with few seeds:** with 3 seeds, seed-level variance estimates are noisy; item-level bootstrap mitigates but power claims must be re-validated from pilot data.

## 3. Justification of key design choices

**(a) Identical episode/token/iteration budgets across arms.** Training quantity is a confounder: more game episodes or more fine-tuning tokens mechanically improves benchmark performance regardless of game type. If arms differed in budget, any observed difference would be attributable to scale of training, not to adversarial vs non-adversarial structure. Therefore: identical number of self-play iterations, identical total fine-tuning tokens (IL + self-play combined), identical data-selection procedures, identical learning-rate schedule, identical decoding parameters at evaluation. Token budgets are matched at the *fine-tuning token* level (not episode count), because average episode length differs across games and episode-count matching would silently create token-count differences.

**(b) GPT-4 imitation held symmetric across arms.** The question fixes IL-on-GPT-4 only for the SPAG arm. Applying IL to all game arms is **Assumption A1** — a deliberate design choice, not a source claim. Justification: if IL were asymmetric, arm differences would conflate (i) game type with (ii) teacher-trajectory exposure. Symmetric IL makes the contrast a clean test of the game structure (adversarial opponent vs cooperative/informational game) under an otherwise identical curriculum. Consequence to acknowledge: a negative result would mean "adversarial games are not superior *under symmetric IL conditions*," not that SPAG's exact recipe (which may rely on the adversarial game specifically for IL) fails. **(c) Superiority test paired with an equivalence check (TOST).** The question is phrased "does A provide superior improvements?" A one-sided superiority test alone cannot distinguish "no difference" from "underpowered study." Pairing a superiority test (one-sided, corrected for multiplicity) with two one-sided tests (TOST) against a pre-registered equivalence margin δ yields a complete 2×2 decision structure: (i) superiority demonstrated; (ii) equivalence demonstrated (adversarial offers no meaningful advantage); (iii) inconclusive (increase power or report honestly). δ should be set a priori, e.g., δ = 1 percentage point accuracy on the primary benchmark composite, or justified by the smallest effect that would matter for a practitioner.

## 4. Addressing the cross-game difficulty/length confounder head-on

The games differ in episode complexity, turn structure, and utterance length; without control, a "better" arm may simply train on more informative or longer text.

Match the *distributions* of these statistics across arms by stratified sampling of training episodes (quantile matching on length and outcome rates), so each arm consumes episodes with comparable statistical profiles.
